passage: The library bell had already rung when Mrs Qureshi found the atlas with its map page torn along the fold. Hafsa was the last one who had borrowed it. "Hafsa, this page was fine last week," Mrs Qureshi said. Hafsa stared at her sandals and said nothing. Her ears went pink. Two boys behind the shelf whispered, "See, she did it." Mrs Qureshi knew silence can mean fear as easily as guilt. She crouched and lowered her voice. "I'm not here to scold you. I just need to know what happened to the page, and then we can mend it." Hafsa's chin wobbled. "It was already loose. I tried to hold it and it ripped more." Mrs Qureshi fetched the clear tape, and they fixed the map together.

qa.q: What did Mrs Qureshi fetch at the end?
qa.a: She fetched the clear tape, and they fixed the map together.

qa.q: What might Hafsa's silence and pink ears suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely she felt scared and embarrassed at being questioned with others listening. The silence did not prove guilt: she later explained the page was already loose.

qa.q: Which choice helped Hafsa speak up, and why?
qa.a: Mrs Qureshi crouched, lowered her voice and said she only needed to know what happened so they could mend it. Taking the shame out made it safe for Hafsa to explain.

qa.q: How did the whispering boys read the silence differently from Mrs Qureshi?
qa.a: The boys took Hafsa's silence as proof that she did it, while Mrs Qureshi knew it might just be fear, so she asked instead of deciding.

grounding: It shows a child's silent, downcast reaction to a reprimand being read as possible fear rather than proof of guilt, and an adult turning to the fix instead of shame.

passage: At the handpump behind the school, Deepu splashed his face and leaned close. "Nirmala told Sir you copied your maths from me. That's why he kept your notebook." Rafiq's fists tightened around his tiffin. He could already picture shouting at her in front of the whole class. Instead he stood still, counting the drips from the spout. "Did you hear her say it?" he asked. Deepu shrugged. "Someone told me." After lunch, Rafiq walked over to Nirmala, who was drawing a kolam pattern on her slate. "Did you tell Sir I copied?" Nirmala looked up, surprised. "No! Sir asked me to collect the notebooks with missing pages. Yours had one." Rafiq's fists opened. That afternoon Sir handed back his notebook with a note: finish page twelve.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq when Deepu told him the rumour?
qa.a: He was at the handpump behind the school.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when his fists tightened around his tiffin?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt, believing Nirmala had got him into trouble, and probably embarrassed that Sir had kept his notebook.

qa.q: What small step stopped the rumour from turning into a fight?
qa.a: Rafiq paused, asked Deepu whether he had heard it himself, and then checked directly with Nirmala instead of shouting at her.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq had shouted at Nirmala in front of the class?
qa.a: Nirmala, who had only collected notebooks, would have been hurt and shamed for something untrue, and a quarrel could have grown out of gossip.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child meeting gossip by pausing, asking for facts and checking with the person involved rather than believing it or hitting back.

passage: For the third Saturday running, Sharmila's towel was missing from the bench at the swimming club, and Avni's group sang "Drippy Sharmila" as she stood shivering by the pool. Avni flicked water at her. "Go on, cry." Sharmila's hands curled. She wanted to push Avni straight into the deep end. Instead she breathed out slowly and walked to the lifeguard's chair, where Coach Latha was writing lap times. "Coach, it keeps happening. The towel, the song, every week." Coach Latha put her clipboard down and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault." Before the session ended, she spoke to Avni's group, found the towel stuffed in a locker, and that evening she rang Sharmila's mother.

qa.q: How many Saturdays in a row had Sharmila's towel gone missing?
qa.a: It was the third Saturday running.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila walk to the lifeguard's chair instead of pushing Avni?
qa.a: She was angry enough to want to push Avni, but she held it in and moved next to a safe adult; she was probably also hurt and tired of the weekly song.

qa.q: How did Coach Latha support Sharmila?
qa.a: She stopped, listened to everything, said it was not Sharmila's fault, and acted the same day: she spoke to the group, found the towel and rang Sharmila's mother.

qa.q: What would change if Sharmila had pushed Avni into the pool?
qa.a: Avni could have been hurt, Sharmila might have been the one blamed, and the repeated taunting could have been hidden behind the push.

grounding: It shows a child recognising repeated taunting as bullying, not hitting back, staying near a safe adult and telling a coach who responds that day.

passage:
"Oye, Professor Wasim! Those new glasses can see the moon from here!" Tarun grinned, tossing the tennis ball.
Wasim pushed the frames up and laughed. "At least I can see your wides, bowler."
"Professor, professor!" chanted Ravi and Kunal from the other end of the lane.
"Okay, okay." Wasim's laugh came out shorter.
"Professor, read the scoreboard with your telescope!" Ravi called again.
Wasim didn't answer. He stared at the ground and missed an easy ball.
Tarun walked up. "You've gone quiet."
"It was funny once," Wasim said. "Not five times. And it's three of you and one of me."
Tarun turned round. "Enough, yaar. Joke's over."
"We were only joking," Kunal said.
"He isn't laughing," Tarun said. "That's how you know." He tossed Wasim the ball. "Sorry. Your bowl."
Wasim half smiled. "Watch out, then."

qa.q: What did Ravi and Kunal chant from the other end of the lane?
qa.a: They chanted "Professor, professor!"

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling once his laugh came out shorter?
qa.a: His laugh came out shorter, he went quiet and missed an easy ball. He enjoyed it at first, but felt hurt and outnumbered once it was repeated by three boys.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that turned things around?
qa.a: He watched Wasim's face rather than the others' laughter, told the group the joke was over, and said sorry.

qa.q: Why might Kunal see the teasing differently from Wasim?
qa.a: Kunal was on the joking side, so it felt harmless to him; Wasim was alone against three, so the same words stung.

grounding: It illustrates playful teasing between friends sliding into mocking when it is repeated and one-sided, and a friend reading the target's face to stop it.

passage:
Tuesday, after school
Today Avni and I nearly stopped being friends over hopscotch. Avni wanted hopscotch at break. I wanted to finish our chalk city on the back steps. We both stood there with our arms folded for ages, and break kept getting shorter.
Then I had an idea. I said, "Hopscotch today, chalk city tomorrow. And on Friday we toss a coin for who picks."
Avni thought about it. "Only if you write it down so you don't forget."
So I wrote it on a page from my rough book and we both signed it like a real contract. Hopscotch was actually fun. I even got to square eight.
The page is folded in my pencil box. Tomorrow is MY turn 😊
- Vidya

qa.q: Where did Vidya put the written deal?
qa.a: The page is folded in Vidya's pencil box.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling while the two friends stood with arms folded?
qa.a: Vidya felt stubborn and also worried, because break kept getting shorter and the quarrel was putting the friendship at risk.

qa.q: Why did writing the deal down help?
qa.a: It turned the promise into something both could remember and check, which was Avni's condition for agreeing, so neither would feel cheated the next day.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt about the deal?
qa.a: Avni probably felt heard and relieved that hopscotch came first, and safer saying yes once the promise was signed 🙂

grounding: It shows a child proposing a turn-taking deal to a friend and the compromise working because both felt heard and the deal was written down to be remembered.

passage:
In their small apartment in Vancouver, Chen dropped his backpack and held up his worksheet like a trophy. "Done. All of it. So can I walk to Leo's by myself?"
His mother, Wei, looked up from the rice cooker. "It's four blocks, and it's getting dark early now."
"Everyone in my class walks alone. Literally everyone."
Wei raised an eyebrow. "Everyone? Maya's dad picks her up every day."
Chen's shoulders dropped. "Okay, most people. But I know the way, and I'll text you when I get there."
Wei nodded slowly. "Finishing your homework is a good reason, and knowing the way is too. The dark is my reason. Go now, text me from Leo's door, and I'll pick you up at six."
Chen was already tying his shoes.

qa.q: How far away is Leo's place?
qa.a: It is four blocks away.

qa.q: Why did Chen's shoulders drop when Wei mentioned Maya's dad?
qa.a: He felt caught out and deflated, because his claim that everyone walks alone was an exaggeration; he still wanted to go, so he offered better reasons.

qa.q: Which part of Wei's reply worked, and why?
qa.a: She took Chen's real reasons seriously, named her own reason, the dark, and set clear limits: go now, text on arrival, pick-up at six 👍

qa.q: What might change if Wei had just said no without explaining?
qa.a: Chen would likely feel dismissed and keep pushing with bigger exaggerations, instead of learning which of his reasons counted.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child using both an exaggerated 'everyone' argument and a valid homework reason, and a parent answering the argument while setting limits.

passage:
The lift in Sai Towers was stuck again, so Chandrika and Keerthana climbed the stairs with their school bags. On the fourth floor, Keerthana stopped. "Tonight at nine, we're all climbing the gate to the closed pool. Everyone from C-block is coming. Say yes now, or you're out. And don't tell anyone."
Chandrika noticed how fast she was talking, and that "everyone" had no names. "Why at night? What's the reason?"
"Because it's fun. Stop asking."
Chandrika said she would think about it. Upstairs, she sat beside Amma, who was cutting beans, and told her everything. Amma put the knife down. "You did right to ask, and right to tell me." Within the hour Amma had spoken to the society guard about the pool gate and called Keerthana's mother.

qa.q: At what time was the group planning to climb the pool gate?
qa.a: At nine that night.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's question about the reason suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and suspicious of the rush, the secrecy and an 'everyone' with no names, though she may also have been worried about being left out.

qa.q: What did Amma do that kept the children safe?
qa.a: She listened, told Chandrika she was right to ask and to tell, and within the hour spoke to the guard about the gate and called Keerthana's mother.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Chandrika's refusal to answer straight away?
qa.a: Keerthana might feel annoyed or let down, since she wanted a quick yes, and later perhaps embarrassed or relieved that an adult stepped in.

grounding: It shows a child spotting 'everyone is doing it' and rush-to-decide pressure, asking for the reason, and telling a trusted adult about a pushed secret dare.

passage:
Monday: Behind the school water tank, Jaya whispered to Harsha that she practised her singing solo in the bathroom because the stage scared her. Harsha hooked her little finger. "Safe with me."
Thursday: Harsha didn't open his tiffin. "A big boy on the van takes my snack money. He said if I tell, I'll see." Jaya's stomach went cold. "This isn't a keep-it secret. Let's go now." At break they found Mrs Iyer, who listened to all of it and said, "It's not your fault, Harsha." Before home time she had called the van in-charge and Harsha's parents.
The next Monday: A teacher rode the van. Harsha sat in the front row of the hall, clapping loudest when Jaya sang.

qa.q: Where did Jaya first share her secret?
qa.a: Behind the school water tank.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when her stomach went cold?
qa.a: Jaya felt frightened for Harsha and alarmed, because unlike her own stage fear this secret was about someone being threatened.

qa.q: Why was Jaya right to treat the two secrets differently?
qa.a: Her stage fear harmed no one, so keeping it built trust; Harsha's secret involved threats and taken money, so it went to a trusted adult the same day.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt when Mrs Iyer said it was not his fault?
qa.a: Harsha likely felt relieved and less alone after being scared into silence by the threat.

grounding: It shows best friends building trust by sharing feelings, and one friend recognising that a secret about harm must go to a trusted adult straight away.

passage: Lokesh, you're asking why I'm not angry about your broken kite? Sit, I'll tell you something. When I was nine, I, Baljeet, the great troublemaker of our lane, sneaked out Bauji's new cycle and scraped it all along a wall. Bauji held up the scratched mudguard. I talked fast: "I did it because Harpal said I couldn't ride a big cycle. And because you never let me. And the wall moved." It all came out at once, some true, some nonsense. Bauji didn't laugh and didn't shout. He asked, "Which reason is the real one?" I went quiet, then admitted I wanted Harpal to stop calling me a baby. Bauji nodded. The next Sunday he taught me to ride that cycle properly, and I polished the mudguard myself.

qa.q: What did young Baljeet scrape along a wall?
qa.a: Bauji's new cycle.

qa.q: Why did young Baljeet give so many reasons at once?
qa.a: Baljeet felt scared and ashamed about the scratch and grabbed at any excuse; underneath was real hurt at being called a baby by Harpal.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Baljeet?
qa.a: Bauji calmly asked which reason was the real one, which let Baljeet name the true need and led to riding lessons instead of punishment.

qa.q: How might Bauji have felt holding up the scratched mudguard?
qa.a: Bauji was probably annoyed about the new cycle, but stayed calm and curious enough to look for the need behind the excuses.

grounding: It illustrates a child's 'I did it because...' mixing real reasons with excuses, and an adult listening for the need behind the explanation.

passage:
Saturday night
Today at Ganga's birthday I told everyone I ate a thousand gulab jamuns, my stomach turned into a hot-air balloon, and I floated over the whole building. Ganga laughed so hard her juice came out of her nose. Then she said she ate two thousand and flew to the moon, and the moon was made of rasmalai 😆 We kept going till her Nani said the ceiling fan would chop us if we floated any higher.
But little Tinku, who is four, asked me very seriously if my tummy still hurt. So I told him, "No, it's a pretend story. I only ate three." He looked relieved and went back to his cake.
Irfan

qa.q: How many gulab jamuns did Irfan really eat?
qa.a: Only three.

qa.q: Why did Irfan tell Tinku it was a pretend story?
qa.a: Irfan felt concerned when Tinku looked worried, and wanted Tinku to know the truth; the tale was only fun while everyone knew it was a joke.

qa.q: What made Irfan's exaggeration play rather than a lie?
qa.a: Everyone at the party knew it was silly and joined in, and when Tinku didn't share the joke, Irfan cleared it up at once.

qa.q: How was the tall tale different for Ganga than for Tinku?
qa.a: Ganga was in on the joke and delighted, adding her own moon story; Tinku didn't share it, so it felt like a real worry until Irfan explained.

grounding: It shows a child telling a tall tale for fun, a friend joining the shared joke, and the child making clear it is not real to a younger child who took it seriously.
